stops.label: Antioch
stops.note: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch in Syria, was arrested during the reign of Trajan (c. 107–110) and condemned to the beasts at Rome. He set out under a guard of ten soldiers, whom he later called “ten leopards” in his letter to the Romans.

stops.label: Philadelphia
stops.note: On the scholarly-accepted northern land route across Asia Minor, Ignatius passed through Philadelphia and met its church; his letter back to it recalls speaking among them. The record of the road between Antioch and Philadelphia is thin — the itinerary is reconstructed from the letters themselves.

stops.label: Smyrna
stops.note: At Smyrna he was received by bishop Polycarp, and delegations from the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, and Tralles came to meet him. From here he wrote four letters: three to those visiting churches and one ahead to Rome, asking the Christians there not to interfere with his death.

stops.label: Troas
stops.note: At the port of Troas he learned that peace had been restored to the church at Antioch, and he wrote three more letters — to Philadelphia, to Smyrna, and to Polycarp personally. He was hurried aboard ship before he could write to the other churches, as the letter to Polycarp notes.

stops.label: Neapolis
stops.note: He sailed from Troas to Neapolis, the Macedonian port — the same crossing Paul made in Acts 16, here in reverse. The stop is known only from a single line in the letter to Polycarp; nothing else of it is recorded.

stops.label: Philippi
stops.note: The church at Philippi received Ignatius and escorted him on his way, then wrote to Polycarp asking for copies of his letters. Polycarp's reply to the Philippians is the source for this stop; beyond Philippi the route to Rome is undocumented.

stops.label: Rome
stops.note: According to early tradition Ignatius was killed by wild beasts in the Roman amphitheater, as he had anticipated in his letter to the Romans. No contemporary account of the death itself survives; the details come from later martyrdom narratives.

letters.title: To the Ephesians
letters.note: Thanks the church of Ephesus for the delegation it sent under bishop Onesimus and urges the congregation to live in harmony with its bishop and with one another.

quote.text: It is better for a man to be silent and be [a Christian], than to talk and not to be one.

letters.title: To the Magnesians
letters.note: Urges the Magnesians to respect their young bishop Damas and warns them against falling back into Jewish practices.

quote.text: It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize.

letters.title: To the Trallians
letters.note: Warns the church of Tralles against teachers who deny that Christ truly was born, suffered, and rose, and holds up the bishop, presbyters, and deacons as the church's ordered center.

quote.text: I therefore, yet not I, but the love of Jesus Christ, entreat you that ye use Christian nourishment only, and abstain from herbage of a different kind; I mean heresy.

letters.title: To the Romans
letters.note: Written ahead to the church at Rome, begging the Christians there not to use their influence to rescue him from the death he saw as his way to God.

quote.text: I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.

letters.title: To the Philadelphians
letters.note: Calls the divided church of Philadelphia back to unity around its bishop and a single shared Eucharist.

quote.text: Take ye heed, then, to have but one Eucharist.

letters.title: To the Smyrnaeans
letters.note: Thanks the church of Smyrna for its hospitality and warns against those who deny that Christ came in the flesh, tying baptism and the Eucharist to the bishop.

quote.text: Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church.

letters.title: To Polycarp
letters.note: A personal letter to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, with counsel on shepherding the church steadily under pressure.

quote.text: Stand firm, as does an anvil which is beaten.
